strengths: Introduces a novel and scientifically interesting task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from a single reader's eye movements, formulated as both candidate selection and open-ended reconstruction.

Uses a substantial public eye-tracking dataset with 360 participants, 486 questions, and multiple observations per question, and evaluates generalization to unseen texts, readers, and both simultaneously.

The strongest discriminative model substantially exceeds chance in three-way selection (49.3% versus 33.0%) and retains similar performance on unseen texts and participants. Mixed-effects testing appropriately recognizes the crossed participant/text structure.

The paper compares several architectures, reports useful difficulty-controlled analyses for questions sharing versus not sharing critical spans, and provides extensive architectural, training, and hyperparameter details.
The limitations and ethical discussion acknowledge reliability, population bias, consent, and privacy concerns associated with eye-tracking applications.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that goals are decoded from eye movements is not adequately isolated. The strongest model receives text, candidate questions, linguistic word properties, and gaze features, but there is no text-only version of that model, zero-gaze ablation, or within-text/participant gaze-shuffling control. Above-chance performance could therefore exploit textual, participant, question-type, or experimental-assignment artifacts rather than goal-conditioned gaze.

The reconstruction evidence generalizes poorly to unseen texts. In the new-text-and-participant regime, agreement with the true question is near zero for question word and semantic category, while BLEU/BERTScore and QA accuracy are comparable to text-only or arbitrary-question baselines. The strong unseen-participant result can partly reflect memorization of the three questions attached to a previously seen text.

No paired significance tests are provided for reconstruction improvements over the text-only and other baselines. Bootstrap intervals for individual scores do not establish that the generally small unseen-text gains are significant.

The cross-validation aggregation is insufficiently specified. Trials appear across multiple test regimes over the ten splits, yet the reported confidence intervals and mixed-effects analysis do not clearly account for repeated test instances, fold dependence, hyperparameter selection, or training-seed variance. Extremely narrow intervals therefore risk overstating certainty.

The manuscript overstates practical readiness and 'open-ended' decoding: the clearest success is three-way discrimination among known candidate questions, whereas genuinely open-ended reconstruction on unseen texts remains weak.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the reproducibility statement ends with a missing dataset URL and provides no code, trained models, exact split files, random seeds, or release commitment. There is also an inconsistency between the main description of DalEye-LLaVA as next-token generation and the appendix description of a candidate-contrastive classification loss.

strengths: The paper studies a novel and scientifically interesting problem: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from reading behavior, extending prior work beyond coarse procedural reading-task classification.
The OneStop dataset is comparatively large for laboratory eye tracking, and the evaluation explicitly considers generalization to unseen participants, unseen texts, and both simultaneously.
The strongest discriminative model produces a meaningful closed-set result: 49.3% three-way accuracy versus 33.0% chance, with gains persisting for unseen texts and participants.
The paper compares several model families, reports confidence intervals and mixed-effects significance tests, and provides useful architectural and hyperparameter details.
The distinction between questions associated with different versus identical critical spans is informative and reveals that fine-grained goal discrimination is substantially harder.
The ethical discussion appropriately recognizes consent, privacy, biometric identification, and possible unreliability for underrepresented reader populations.
weaknesses: The essential attribution claim is insufficiently supported. There is no text-and-question-only ablation, gaze-shuffling or permutation control, feature-group ablation, or participant-mean control for the strongest model. Consequently, the experiments do not establish which gaze information drives performance or adequately rule out dataset and preprocessing artifacts.

The framing substantially overstates the demonstrated scope. Selection is among exactly three known questions constructed under a special two-critical-span design, rather than arbitrary open-ended goals. Moreover, the models receive the paragraph and, for selection, all candidate questions, so the repeated claim that goals are decoded 'solely from eye movements' is inaccurate.

Evidence for open-ended reconstruction on genuinely unseen texts is poor. In the New Text regime, question-word and category kappas are only 0.069 and 0.074; the model loses to an incorrect same-span human question on BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy, and its 65.1% QA accuracy is also below the arbitrary GPT-4o baseline's 66.7%. Strong results when the text was seen during training can largely reflect memorization of its three fixed questions.

The reconstruction metrics do not convincingly measure recovery of the intended goal. BLEU and BERTScore are unreliable with one reference, while the proposed QA metric awards high scores to arbitrary or incorrect questions and is evaluated only on the 86% subset already answered correctly by another model. Human judgments of semantic equivalence are absent.

The strongest fine-grained claim is modest: same-span accuracy is 57.3% versus 49.9% chance overall, and the unseen-text-and-participant result is not statistically above chance. That hardest regime constitutes only 1% of each split, limiting confidence in generalization.

The cross-validation accounting is insufficiently clear. The paper states that most trials appear in both New Participant and New Text evaluations across the ten splits, yet aggregates predictions into very tight confidence intervals without explaining how repeated test predictions and heavily overlapping training sets are handled statistically. Random effects for participant and paragraph do not transparently resolve dependence caused by repeated trial predictions.

There are methodological inconsistencies affecting reproducibility: DalEye-LLaVA is described as autoregressive next-token training in the main text and teacher forcing in one appendix section, but elsewhere as a contrastive candidate-likelihood classification objective. Stochastic training variance, seeds, released split identifiers, and code availability are also not reported; the reproducibility statement ends with an incomplete dataset link.

The evaluation is restricted to one English dataset, one laboratory setup, one high-end eye tracker, and a setting where readers explicitly see a comprehension question immediately before reading. This is far from the real-time, naturally occurring information needs invoked in the proposed educational, accessibility, media, and government-service applications.

Overall, the novel task and closed-set result are promising, but the missing causal/ablative controls and the failure of reconstruction on unseen texts leave the central claims under-supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel and scientifically interesting task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from a single reader's eye movements, including both candidate selection and open-ended reconstruction.

The evaluation uses a substantial public eye-tracking dataset and thoughtfully separates generalization to unseen readers, unseen texts, and both. Article-level partitioning reduces topical leakage across paragraphs.

The strongest selection results are convincing: RoBERTEye-Fixations achieves 49.3% accuracy versus 33.0% chance overall, 70.9% versus 55.3% across different critical spans, and 57.3% versus 49.9% for the particularly informative same-span condition. Improvements are consistent across generalization regimes and supported by mixed-effects analyses.

The study compares heuristic, recurrent, transformer-based, and generative approaches; reports confidence intervals, detailed hyperparameters, input-representation variations, and several complementary reconstruction metrics.

The paper is clearly motivated and well positioned relative to psycholinguistics and gaze-based cognitive-state decoding. It also explicitly discusses consent, privacy, reliability, and population-bias risks.
weaknesses: The discriminative experiments lack matched text-only, gaze-shuffled, or gaze-permuted ablations. Although balanced labels make strong text-only performance unlikely, these controls are important for establishing that gains arise from goal-dependent gaze signals rather than preprocessing artifacts, memorization, or other correlations.

Open-ended reconstruction generalizes weakly to unseen texts. For New Text, DalEye-Llama obtains only 0.069 question-word kappa and 0.074 category kappa, while the same-span human baseline is better on BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy. The strongest reconstruction result occurs when the text was seen during training, where the fixed question set can be memorized; claims of precise free-form reconstruction should therefore be tempered.

The New Text & Participant test portion is only 1% per split. Moreover, trials can appear under multiple evaluation regimes across the ten splits, but it is unclear whether confidence intervals and mixed-effects tests account for repeated predictions of the same trial or fold-level dependence.

The description of DalEye-LLaVA's objective is inconsistent: the main text describes autoregressive training on the correct question, whereas Appendix C describes contrastive optimization over the correct question and two distractors. This matters for interpreting it as an open-ended generative model.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or fold assignments are provided, random seeds and repeated-run variability are not reported, and the dataset URL in the reproducibility statement appears blank. Overall, the paper is competitive and merits acceptance, but these omissions keep it below a clear Accept score.

strengths: Introduces a novel and scientifically interesting task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from gaze, including both candidate selection and open-ended reconstruction.
Uses a substantial public eye-tracking dataset with 180 information-seeking participants, 162 paragraphs, 486 questions, and critical-span annotations.
The evaluation explicitly considers generalization to unseen participants, unseen texts, and both simultaneously, with article-level separation to reduce textual leakage.

RoBERTEye-Fixations produces a clear selection result: 49.3% three-way accuracy versus 33.0% chance, including 57.3% versus 49.9% when distinguishing questions sharing a critical span. Performance remains similar on unseen texts and participants.
The paper includes multiple baselines, feature ablations, confidence intervals, mixed-effects analyses, alternative gaze representations, and several reconstruction metrics.
The analysis relating decoding performance to reading inside versus outside critical spans is cognitively interpretable and connects the predictive results to prior psycholinguistic findings.
The manuscript is clear, well organized, and unusually detailed about prompts, features, hyperparameters, model versions, and ethical risks.
weaknesses: The main technical methods are largely adaptations of existing gaze-text architectures or textual prompting/fine-tuning of existing LLMs. The strongest contribution is therefore the task and evaluation rather than a substantial modeling advance.

The open-ended reconstruction evidence is considerably weaker than the framing suggests. On unseen texts, improvements over text-only counterparts are generally small, sometimes absent, and generated models often lose to an incorrect human question sharing the critical span on BLEU and BERTScore.

No human evaluation establishes whether generated questions recover the reader's intended information need. Question-word accuracy, BLEU, BERTScore, and coarse automatically assigned categories are imperfect proxies for semantic goal equivalence.

The downstream QA metric has limited specificity: it evaluates only the 86% of items already answered correctly by a separate QA model and can reward unrelated questions because that model also sees the original passage and answer choices. Strong scores from incorrect-human and zero-shot baselines illustrate this limitation.

The cross-validation aggregation appears to reuse many trials across evaluation regimes and folds: the paper states that 90% of trials appear in both the New Participant and New Text regimes. The mixed-effects tests do not clearly model repeated predictions of the same trial or cross-validation dependence, making the very narrow confidence intervals and extreme p-values difficult to interpret.

The crucial New Text & Participant test comprises only 1% of each split. In the difficult same-span condition, its apparent improvement is not shown to be statistically significant, weakening the strongest claim of fine-grained generalization.

The feature ablation does not cleanly isolate conventional gaze measurements. Removing all fixation-level feature values still retains the fixation sequence and its alignment to word positions, which itself contains substantial gaze information; correspondingly, most explicit feature ablations produce only small changes.

Results come from one English dataset, one reading-comprehension collection, one laboratory eye tracker, and a constrained three-question design. This limits evidence for the paper's broader claims about arbitrary real-world goals, real-time assistance, and general reading interfaces.

The privacy discussion is welcome but incomplete given the proposed applications: inferred information needs can be sensitive, and deployment would require analysis of consent, inference misuse, demographic bias, calibration, and failures beyond the brief caveats provided.

strengths: The paper introduces an interesting and relatively novel problem: inferring a reader's information-seeking goal from gaze behavior, with both selection and generation formulations.
The OneStop data provide substantial experimental structure: 360 participants, 162 paragraphs, 486 questions, repeated observations, and manually annotated critical spans.

The strongest selection result is meaningful: RoBERTEye-Fixations obtains 49.3% three-way accuracy versus 33% chance, including 57.3% when distinguishing questions associated with the same critical span.
Evaluation distinguishes generalization to unseen participants, texts, and both, with article-level separation intended to limit textual leakage.
The cognitive analysis is useful: decoding improves when readers spend relatively more time in the task-critical span, connecting model behavior to established findings about goal-directed reading.
The appendix provides extensive implementation details, feature ablations, numerical results, prompts, and ethical discussion.
weaknesses: The central framing substantially overstates the demonstrated capability. Selection is restricted to three supplied questions per passage, while reconstruction targets one of only 486 dataset-authored questions. This is much narrower than decoding arbitrary or open-ended goals.

The impressive reconstruction results primarily occur for new participants when the same passage and its questions have appeared during training, allowing substantial question memorization. On unseen texts, gaze-conditioned improvements are generally small, inconsistent across metrics, and sometimes absent or negative.

Crucial controls are missing. The paper does not test scanpaths shuffled among questions for the same passage, randomized fixation order, mismatched durations, or an otherwise identical selection model without gaze. The reported ablations retain the gaze-derived ordering of word embeddings, so they do not establish which information actually supports decoding or rule out shortcuts.

Gemini few-shot lacks a matched text-only few-shot baseline using the same demonstrations with gaze removed or permuted. Comparing it with an arbitrary zero-shot Gemini question does not isolate the contribution of eye movements.

The reconstruction evaluation is not convincing enough for the main claim. There is no blinded human assessment of whether generations express the intended information need, and only one reference question is used. Question-word and category accuracy are coarse; BLEU and BERTScore penalize valid paraphrases; and the QA metric can reward an unrelated question whenever the downstream model selects the correct answer.

The weakness of these metrics is visible empirically: an explicitly incorrect human question sharing the critical span frequently surpasses gaze-conditioned systems on BLEU, BERTScore, or QA accuracy for unseen texts. Thus the reported scores do not reliably demonstrate recovery of the precise goal.

The cross-validation aggregation is insufficiently justified statistically. The manuscript states that 90% of trials appear in both the new-participant and new-text regimes across splits, yet uncertainty estimates do not appear to model repeated trial predictions or variation across training runs. No multi-seed robustness is reported despite fine-tuning large neural models.

The methodological novelty is limited: most systems are adaptations or prompt-based fine-tuning of existing architectures. The principal novelty is the task formulation, which makes the lack of decisive controls and robust open-ended evaluation especially consequential.

Claims about practical educational, accessibility, and personalization applications are premature given modest accuracy, laboratory-grade eye tracking, a homogeneous native-English sample, and no evaluation of demographic, impairment-related, device, or domain shift.

strengths: Introduces a novel and meaningful task: decoding arbitrary, text-specific information-seeking goals from a single reader’s eye movements, formulated as both candidate selection and free-form reconstruction.
Uses a valuable large-scale eye-tracking dataset with hundreds of questions, manually annotated critical spans, and repeated observations across 360 participants.

The evaluation carefully distinguishes generalization to new participants, new texts, and both simultaneously, with article-level text splitting and mixed-effects significance tests that account for participant and paragraph structure.

Goal-selection results are convincing: RoBERTEye-Fixations substantially exceeds chance overall (49.3% versus 33.0%) and retains comparable performance for unseen texts and participants. Above-chance discrimination between questions sharing the same critical span is particularly interesting.

The paper compares several discriminative and generative approaches, includes text-only and human-question controls, reports multiple reconstruction metrics, and provides useful feature, prompt, and input-representation ablations.
The analysis connecting decoding success to reading time inside versus outside the critical span is cognitively interpretable and provides scientific value beyond raw predictive performance.
The manuscript is clear, well organized, and unusually thorough about model architecture, training, statistical testing, and ethical risks.
weaknesses: The open-ended reconstruction claim is strongest in the new-participant regime, where the same texts and their possible questions occur during training. Exact or near-exact reconstruction there can substantially reflect memorization. On genuinely new texts, performance drops sharply and improvements over text-only controls are often small or inconsistent.

Reconstruction quality remains ambiguous. BLEU and BERTScore reward lexical overlap, UIUC categories are coarse and automatically assigned, and the QA metric supplies answer options belonging to the true question and excludes the 14% of items the evaluator cannot originally answer. Human judgments of semantic equivalence or goal recovery would provide much stronger evidence.

The selection ablation indicates that most performance survives removal of explicit fixation, word-level gaze, saccade, or linguistic feature groups. The paper attributes substantial signal to fixation-ordered lexical embeddings, but does not directly compare against decisive controls such as shuffled scanpaths, scanpaths from another participant/question, or fixation sequences with durations and other measurements removed. These controls are important for identifying what eye-tracking information actually drives decoding.

The same-span selection result is statistically reliable but modest in magnitude (57.3% versus 50%), and it is not significant in the small jointly unseen participant-and-text subset. Some practical and fine-grained claims should therefore be tempered.

The jointly unseen regime constitutes only about 1% of each split, producing relatively uncertain estimates. Repeated cross-validation predictions may also reuse observations across regimes, while the reported inferential models do not clearly include trial identity or model-training randomness.

The cognitive analysis is correlational and partly involves strongly related reading-time predictors. Extremely small p-values do not establish the proposed causal interpretations, and robustness or multicollinearity diagnostics are not reported.

The reproducibility statement claims that data and code are available, but the corresponding links are absent in the submitted PDF. Reproduction of commercial-model experiments will additionally depend on API versions and unavailable model internals.

Although the ethics section appropriately discusses consent and demographic reliability, goal inference from gaze creates substantial privacy and surveillance risks; the discussion could more fully address misuse, secondary inference, data retention, and deployment safeguards.
